From the Barbados Mercury, August 10. The arrival of her Majesty's packet Reindeer on Wednesday morning last, put us in possession of London and other English tiles to the 15th ultimo The mortal remains of our late good and gracious Monarch, W tlliam the Fourth, were interred on the 8th ultimo. in St. George's Chapel, Windsor Every tribute of affectionate regard, which an afflicted people could pay the memory of a beloved Sovereign, was observed upon the melancholy occasion. Never did the tomb which has closed over his late Majesty, receive within its confines a better Monarch or a better man. In him the nation possessed a truly merciful and just ruler; he was a warm and generous patron to the Army and Navy, and ever ready to reward merit in both branches of the service, to the utmost ot his power JBy all his subjects, indeed, will the memory of William the Good be held in reverence and respect, but by none more so than the inhabitants of this island, where they will ever have the proud boast that his late Majesty passed part of his youthful career, while serving in the Navy. Her Majesty the Queen Dowager did not attend the funeral procession, but witnessed the mournful ceremony from the Queen's closet, which adjoins the altar in the Ghapel. After the funeral Iter Majesty quitted for Bushy. We observe that Viscount Melbourne bad been frequently honoured by Iter Majesty with an audience þÿ in some cases his Lordship remained at the l'alace for upwards oi two hours

The Parliament was to have been prorogued on Tuesday the 18th ultimo. It was not known whether her Majesty would perform the ceremony herself. Her Majesty intended to open the new parliament, and deliver the address from the Throne. The approaching general election was looked forward to with that intense interest which a political struggle of such great importance to the whole nation, may well be supposed to have created. The friends and supporters of the opposing parties, as usual, seem quite confident of success. It looks as if the conservatives would make a strong muste.r : they are often given as candidates, two to one against the Liberals. In Bristol the conservative cause had every prospect of triumphing Prince Napoleon Louis Bonaparte, who had been sent from France America, to had arrived in London from New York. I he illness of his mother, the ex Queen Hortense, Duchess of St. Leu, it is said, has occasioned his return to Europe. Extract of a Despatch from the President of Tortola. dated August 5th, 1837. "It is with feelings of the deepest sorrow that I have to communicate to your Excellency the account of a most calamitous event which occurred here on the 2nd instant, occasioning to the inhabitants such suffering and distress as it is not in my power to convey an adequate description of. It pleased Almighty God to visit us w ith a Hurricane equalling in violence that of 1811), and producing the most appalling effects : þÿ it commenced about 3 o'clock in the afternoon,

and continued with increased violence until about 9 o'clock at night, when it began to abate : but the following morning presented a scene of great misery and distress, many houses in the Road-town were blown down and destroyed, and several of those that were left standing are much injured. In the country, several sots of sugar-works, dwellinghouses, and other buildings, that withstood the Hurricane of 1819. are levelled with the earth : all the negro houses, negro grounds, fruit tree.s, <vc., throughout the island, are rompictoly destroyed ; and the canes are so much injured, that I much fear little return can be expected from them the next season, jf even the works, and other necessary buildings can be rebuilt, which, from the present impoverished of state of the inhabitants, unless probability being accomplished, I see no assistance can be obtained from some quarter. þÿ All the buildings at the African location, with the exception of 0 or 7, have also been blown down.

"1 enclose a report which 1 have just received from Mr Special Magistrate Gordon, detailing the effects of this awful calamity, which lias come under his immediate observation, and which 1 am much concerned to be enabled to corroborate." From the St. Christopher Advertiser, Aug. 5. Extract of a letter from St. Martins, dated August 10: þÿ " li commenced about 9 o'clock in the morning, and raged with great violence from 11 to 2 p m., veering from E N. E toN. Colonial Bank. þÿ The Branch Bank for this Island will he opened next Tuesday, the 1st August. All the necessary preparations having been made þÿ a fire proof vault has been erected, and every precaution taken to secure the trust reposed" in the Director here. A supply of Cash was received here by the Post Boat that brought down the 1st June Mail þÿ One of the Directors lit si appointed, William Gowan, Esq , we regret to state has resigned ; the Bank, we believe, will he conducted oy one Director only, James Berridgc, Esq , whose long with matters, combined experience in monetary his unremitting attention, give earnest proot that the business will he welt managed, and we congratulate the community on the opening of so desirable an establishment. þÿ St. Christopher Gazette, July 28.

We are happy in having this day to announce the opening in this Island, of so important a Mercantile Institution, as the Colonial Bank. The establishment of this Institution indicates in British Capitalists a firm confidence in West Indian resources, and consequently in the industry by which such resources must he furnished. To every member of the community such an Institution may he a matter of profit or convenience, it will enlarge the amount of Currency in circulation þÿ afford to small dealers of integrity the means of extending their business þÿ supply the agriculturist with funds for the periodical payment of his labourers þÿ and afford professional men, and private individuals, a safe and advantageous investment of accumulation from their income. Wc understand that William Gowan. Esq., has withdrawn front the directorship, hut we have not yet learned the name of his successor, if it he contemplated to fill up his vacancy. '1 he sole director therefore at present is James Bcrridge, Esq., whose business like habits are so well-known as to need no eulogium from us. þÿ Saint Christopher Advertiser. August 1. He saw, fluttering in the air, a piece of cloth of a prodigious length, composed of all the cabbage he had made, of a variety of colours. The Angel of death held this piece of patchwork in one of his hands, and with the other gave the tailor several strokes with a piece of iron. 1 he tailor awakening in a fright, made a vow, that it he recoveicd he would cabbage no more. Ho soon recovered. As lie was diffident in himself lie ordered one of his apprentices to put him in mind of his dream, whenever he cut out a suit of clothes. The tailor was for some time obedient to the intimations given him by his apprentice. Temperance we have always been taught to consider a virtue, and as virtue is a jewel of inestimable value, we canaot but advocate the strictest observance of the practice. In this as well as in most of these islands, tem- " perance Societies have been establishes, but whether their good effects are vet observable, we pretend not to determine To reclaim, the habitual drunkard, and convert the licentious rather husband, brother, or friend from a course of vice, which leads to penury,

We read every day of converts to these societies, of the good which the newly initiated have experienced after a short trial, and the benefits derivable from an implicit observance of those rules ; yet 9trangc to say, crime of every grade stalks through the land with undiminished strides. Gevernor but as an Advocate for the interests of this Colony þÿ I have travelled in many parts of the civilised and uncivilised world, amongst barbarians and savages þÿ and have invariably found filth, laziness, ignorance and presumption to pervade the dwellings of uncivilized men. " The soul is of no colour but the body be it white, black or brown can scarcely be said to contain a soul without some degree of education and moral as well as religious restraint þÿ Man indeed alone sinks below the brute creation, when uncivilized. " Jf there he a race of men so blind to the interests ol humanity as to discouiage education þÿ let liiein cherish their error if they please þÿ but let those who have wiser and more enlightened sentiments pursue with perseverance a more nobie course. "We are called on to-day, to express our determination to uphold Education þÿ to unite our eliorts with our respected Pastor, and enable the children of the poorer inhabitants to obtain habits of discipline, industry and self command. þÿ The doctrines of our Saviour teacti these habits þÿ To be ol use those doctrines must be made familiar þÿ they cannot be familiar þÿ unless read þÿ to read them must be through the aid ol teachers þÿ and teachers must be paid. " When education is general þÿ no person will pride himself on a little knowledge þÿ n is

only when the few are instrucied liiat the desire to escape irom manual labour arises in tiie mind of those who have only the rudiments of knowledge. " The Peasants of Protestant Savoy þÿ of Switzerland, ot Scotland, mountainous countries like this, all read their Bibles, and yet few nations can be compared with them lor bodily exertion and manual labours. " 1 Ins Colony suffers under the difficulty ot intercourse between its inhabitants þÿ Education must perhaps be at first confined to those parts where such intercourse is free þÿ \ ou have began with the town þÿ begin now with its neighbourhood þÿ The circle will lie gradually extended till at last the necessity and demand for education, will level forests þÿ traverse mountains and unite all breasts in one bond þÿ his precepts for our Rule þÿ with our Saviour for llie guide þÿ " Bar. I he following description of the Hurricane of the 2d iiislant, by the Captain of the H titer Witch, is extracted from Monday's Globe: St. Thomas, August Hilt 1837. "1 left Liverpool on the 19th June, and after a long and tedious passage arrived oil this port on the 2nd Instant. The morning of that day was ushered in with squally weather; the Water Witch was off' St. John's Island, standing down for St Thomas, wind N. and iN. N. VV. ; about mid-day the harbor and a quantity of shipping were visible; i about 1 r. m the sqalls were violent, and brought us under double reeled topsails, lore-

sails, and trysails; at 3 p. m the vessel had beat up within half a mile of the f i ts at the entrance of the harbor, when the squalls were so frequent and violent, we could proceed no farther, consequently came to anciior m 10 fathoms water; sent down top gallant yards, and struck the masts, and made every preparation for an approaching Gale þÿ Hurricane 1 saw no signs of. About 5 p. m. the squalls had ceased and terminated in a heavy Gale, but with the wind oil' the land, I did not much mind it, as J had good ground tackle : but at 6 p. m. she took the anchor on her shoulder, and marched away with it ; the 2nd was let go, and both cables veered < >ut end for end þÿ the vessel still driving. At 7 the Hurricane was beyond all description dreadful ; every thing before it disappeared. At this time the windlass capsized, and the chains were fast below, round the mainmast, so that 1 could not slip them ; all we could do was to hold on, sink at our anchors, or part cables ; the latter 1 wished she would do, but they were too good for that, and glad ain 1 to sav thev bore me through the terrible Gale, She continued driving until 3 p. m. ; she was then in 20 lathoms water, hut going directly on Buck Island; a calm now ensued for about 10 minutes, and then in the most tremendous unearthly screech I ever heard, it recommenced with redoubled fury, at S. and S. W. ; 1 now considered it all up with us, for the wind was directly on the shore, and ihe sea rose, and ran mountains high. About half

past 9 the bob-stay gave way ; I expected the masis to follow, hut they held on ; the fore royal mast (a 1 1 ho' struck) blew off, the fore topsail yard broke, and the gig at the quarter was taken lip as if on " Eagles wings," carried some feet in the air, and then was borne before the blast, as tho' it had been a sheet ol paper ! The Vessel continued to drive, and got into 12 fathoms again þÿ and then held on. We were obliged to steer her all night, to keep her head to the wind, lor (when she got her hows to it, she went down on her broadside;) in doing which, 1 have got my left arm dreadfully bruised, and my thumb sprained ; one man bad his arm broken, and thigh much bruised, and a third his wrist sprained, occasioned by a tremendous plunge, which took the wheel from our hands þÿ this of course rendered us useless lor the rest of the night. About 2 a m. the Gale abated somewhat, and the Barometer rose an inch ; this was warmly hailed by me you may he sure. Daylight came, and although the Gale was much abated, yet it still blew with great violence, directly on the land. We now began to repair the windlass, which was effected after a hard day's work, and got up our anchors, & ane, bored in the harbour about 5 p. m ; þÿ but hero what, a sight was presented to my view, out of 40 vessels which but 24 hours previously, had towered their lofty pines on high, but one alone, and ourselves, remained; "all" having sunk, gone on shore, and been dashed to pieces, orr.apsizc.il, Hew we held on I cannot say, it is a miracle ;

altho' we have received no injury in the hull, yet our masts, yards, rigging, and sails have received much, hut these arc trifles, light as air, compared with ;hose around mo. St. Croix, CHRIS TIA i\ S TE D, (MONDAY) September 11, 1837. We have been favored with the perusal of London papers of the 3tst July, pr. first August packet. Great Britain was in the midst of a general election for members of Parliament. In England many of the elections were over, and the gains and losses of each party are nearly balanced. London (in every district), Manchester, Birmingham, Leeds, with many other boroughs, have all returned Liberal members. In Liverpool and Bath and many other places, the conversative candidates are successful. General Evans, is re-elected for Westminister, with Mr. Leader, who was unsuccessfully opposed by Sir George Murray. In Edinborough, Glasgow, Paisley, Aberdeen þÿ&c liberal members are returned but many places in England, Scotland and Ireland had not yet chosen their members. It is supposed that the strength of parties will be nearly similar, in the new House of Commons to the oid one. In Spain Oroa gained a victory over Don Carlos on the 15th July þÿ the latter had advanced to within a league of Valencia, which however, he did not enter ; the inhabitants shewing no disposition to join him ; Uma advanced, and threw himsell into Valencia ; a battle ensued, which resulted in the rapid retreat and defeat of the Carlists who were hastening to recross the Ebro. The King of Sweden was considered in a very precarious slate, and his decease daily expected. A military revolt had broke out in Portugal among the troops. The Cholera was raging badly at Naples & at Palermo in Sicily ; in the former 700 and

in the latter 12 or 15,00 deaths occurred daily þÿ the sick and dead were abandoned by the þÿinhabitants, in Malta it prevailed badly and Sir J. Rowley with his licet of several ships of the line, had put to sea, in consequence. The prevailing impression appears to be that commerce will now gradually revive, and confidence, which of late has been so seriously diminished, is slowly returning We are still without any fresh stoppages to shake or engender its improvement, and it may now be presumed that we are again upon solid ground. The following is related as a dialogue between a drunkard and his wife ; it is in perfect accordance with the unreasonableness of drunkards in general. I say, Molly, what have you got for dinner V ' 1 told you, this morning, we had nothing in the house.' O, well, let me take the baby, and you pick up something.' ' 8o you told mc this morning, but there's nothing to pick up.' 'Oh pick up some hread and potatoes, Molly, pick up something.' ' Rut Mr. Lindsey, there's nothing in the house.' þÿ Nothing at all.' No meal, nor bread, nor butter, nor potatoes, nor a mouthful of any thing that can he eaten.' ' Well, well, Molly, 1 say pick up a little something or other, and let us have dinner, for I am in a hurry,'

Valuable Hints. þÿ A patch on the elbow, poor Richard said þÿ and he knew something þÿ is better than a dun at the elbow. Don't order a new pair of boots until you have put the last patch on the old ones. Don't discard an old garment for a new fashion. If you are poor, it is some consolation that you can shave yourself. Avoid the man who says the world owes him a living. A new sot of buttons revives an old coat.

The ordinance of 11th Novb. 1776, 16th July 1778, 13th April 1770, 16th March 1792, and the 1st Oct. 1802, together with the governor general's placard of the 10th Nov, 1823, with the exception of the instalments for paying the capitation tax have laid down tiie manner in which payment of taxes on properties in the westindies are to be paid, and the following rules are to be observed: That Negroes willfully not given up by their owners or by those persons in whose possession thev arc, will be sold for account of the king, and the informer, if any. The capitation tax to the royal treasury is Glsk. W. C. for each town negro and Ps. 1 32sk for each male negro in the country, and to the land treasury Ps 1 for caciitown negro and Ps. 2 for each male negro in the country, to be paid thus: Capitation lax not amounting

®A.»8:K fMt»B>18gL WMmWH AT33% to Ps: 20 immediately on taking up the list, hut if Ps. 20 and above that sum, in the manner specified in the ordinance of the 11th November 1176. That negroes born or dead in the course of the year, are not taxable, but they are notwithstanding to be regularly specified in the lists delivered. þÿ All other negroes are taxable, includiug invalids. Exact lists of the town negroes together with increase or decrease are to be delivered to the commissioners. In like manner the lists of the estates must be made out with a true specification of the number of acres in canes, or in any other cultivation or pasture, the number of acres not used and the number of acres entirely useless þÿ In consequence whereof, the royal governments publication of the 26th of September 1833 is to be attended to ; Furthermore the names of the present owners, (as directed for the towns) together with the names of all the inhabitants without exception, are to be specified on the lists. For the convenience of the community, and in order to obtain as much regularity, as possible in the tax lists, schemes have been made printed by the Royal vvestindia government, which schemes will be delivered gratis for the town of Christianstaed and its Jurisdiction, at the burgher councils Incassator office and in Frederikstcd and its Jurisdictional the police office of that town. It is a duty incumbent on every owner of a house to announce himself as such, in writing to the commission to prevent any doubt who is to pay the house tax ; and it is further di-

rected, that owners of houses, that have been vacant or untenanted for six months or upwards, and in consequence thereof are entitled to get a proportional reduction in their taxes, are for that purpose, to come forward with sufficient proof of their assertion in order to enable the commissioners to observe the needful in the protocol ; in which respect the Commissioners refer to the royal Governments publication of 20th October, 1836. It is to be observed, that the commission will receive no tax lists, except they are made out according to the above mentioned schemes, and every column properly filled up. It is however understood, that such lists are not required from owners of houses, who have od!v to announce themselves as such to the commission, though not occupying their liousees, as in such cases it will be considered sufficient when they announce themselves as such, together with the names of the persons who occupy the house, in writing to the commissioners. Separate lists duly signed by the owner or occupier for each house or plantation, is to be delivered to the commission notwithstanding the concerned individual might own more than one house or plantation. All houses in both towns are to be numbered, and the name of the streets to be placed on both sides of the oornerhouses, painted with white on black ground or vice versa, in a conspicuous manner, according to Governor General v. Ceausens placard of the 4th January 1777. In case of non compliance with the above,

the following lines are to be paid and levied for : Ten Pieces of Eight for every list that is not rendered in due time, it be cither in town or country, and proprietors, giving in lists which do not contain the explanations directed according to the beforcmcntioned schemes

w ill he subjected to the same fine, as the lists, in such cases will be returned to them. Owners of houses in towns, who neglect announcing themselves as such in writing are liable to the same fine. 10 Ps. for every house number that is either wanted or illegible, and the same for every streets name having the same defect. For all unpaid capitation tax under Ps. 20 a levy will he made within 24 hours after the time, when the lists ought to have been delivered to the commissioners. Furthermore all persons are requested to bring the exact amount of the capitation tax to be paid to each treasury, as the time will not allow to make change. THE LITTLE MAID. I There was a little maid Who wore a little bonnet, And she had a little finger With a little ring upon it. She screwed her little waist, To such a little size, That it made her little blood Rush to her little eyes.

This pretty little maid Had a pretty little beau, Who wore a little hat And gloves as white as snow, He said his little heart, Was in a little flutter, þÿ That he loved the little maid, And no one else but her.

She smiled a little smile, When he breathed his little vows, And he kissed her little hand, With man\r little bows. By little and by little Her little heart did yield. Till little tears and sighs, Her little fears revealed 1

A little while þÿ alas T And her little beau departed, With all his little vows, And left her broken hearted. Now, all ye little maids, A moral I will give you ; l)on't trust to little men, They surely will deceive you.

The merchants here, without a solitary exception, deprecate in the most decided terms the plan laid down in tlie þÿmessage. The Widow's Woe. þÿ Last evening, two genteelly dressed young women, one of whom was in deep mourning, entered the Police Office, and asked to see the Coroner. The Coroner happened not to be in his office at the moment, and the two ladies were shown into an inner room to await his arrival. After waiting a few minutes, the lady in black, whose name turned out to he Mrs Mc'Avoirty, whose accent left no doubt of her Hibernian origin, addressed a gentleman who was standing in the room, and in a very subdued tone of voice and manner, asked him if the Coroner would shortly come in. The gentleman replied that it was quite uncertain, as it depended entirely on circumstances. Mrs. Mo'Avoirty. Do you think he will come here at all this evening' 1 want to see him very badly. Gentleman. Do you want him to hold an inquest ? Mrs. Me'A. I want him sir, in relation to my husband, that was drowned in the North river. Gentleman. Indeed! When washe drowned ? Mrs. Me'A. The ordinance of lllhNovb. 1776, 10th July 1778, 13th April 1779, 16th March 1792, and the 1st Oct. 1802, together with the governor general's placard of the 10th Nov. 1823, with the exception of the instalments for paying the capitation tax have laid down the manner in which payment of taxes on properties in the westindies arc to be paid, and i he following rules are to be observed: That Negroes willfully not given up by their owners or by those persons in whose possession they arc, will be sold for account of the king, and the informer, if any. The capitation tax to the royal treasury is 61.sk W. 0. for each town negro and Ps. 1 32sk. for each male negro in the country, and to the land treasury Ps 1 for each town negro and l's. 2 for each male negro in the country, to be paid thus : Capitation tax not amounting

In like manner the lists of the estates must be made out with a true specification of the number of acres in canes, or in any other cultivation or pasture, the number of acres not used and the number of acres entirely useless þÿ In Consequence whereof, the royal governments publication of the 26 tli of September 1833 is to be attended to ; Furthermore the names of the present owners, (as directed for the towns) together with the names of all the inhabitants without exception, are to be specified on the lists. For the convenience of the community, and in order to obtain as much regularity, as possible in the tax lists, schemes have been made printed by the Royal westinaia government, which schemes will be delivered gratis for the town of Christianstaed and its Jurisdiction, at tbe burgher councils Incassator ofiice and in Frederikstcd and its Jurisdiction at the police ofiice of that town. It is a duty incumbent on every owner of a house to announce himself as such, in writing to the commission to prevent any doubt who is to pay the house tax ; and it is further di-

rected, that owners of houses, that have been vacant or untenanted for six months or upwards, and in consequence thereof are entitled to get a proportional reduction in their taxes, are for that purpose, to come forward with sufficient proof of their assertion in order to enable the commissioners to observe the needful in the protocol ; in which respect the Commissioners refer to the royal Governments publication of 20th October, 1836. It is to be observed, that the commission will receive no tax lists, except they are made out according to the above mentioned schemes, and every column properly filled up. It is however understood, that such lists are not required from owners ot houses, who have only to announce themselves as such to the commission, though not occupying their housecs, as in such cases it will be considered sufficient when they announce themselves as such, together with the names of the persons who occupy the house, in writing to the commissioners. Separate lists duly signed by the owner or occupier for each house or plantation, is to be delivered to the commission notwithstanding the concerned individual might own morethan one house or plantation. All houses in both towns are to be numbered, and tbe name of the streets to be placed on both sides of the corncrhouses, painted with white on black ground or vice versa, in a conspicuous manner, according to Governor General v. the following fines are to be paid and levied for : Ten Pieces of Eight for every list that is not rendered in due time, it be either in town or country, and proprietors, giving in lists which do not contain the explanations directed according to the Leforemcnlioned schemes

will bo subjected to the same fine, as the list!; in Such cases will be returned to lliim. From the New York Express, monday morning october 16, 1837. THIRTEEN DAYS LATER FROM EUROPE. The Packet ship Orpheus, Capt. Rurslcy, arrived at this port on Saturday, bringing us our files of London and Liverpool papers. þÿ The former arc to the 15th and the latter to 16th September inclusive. We find little in our papers of importance. Parliament had been prorogued to the 2d October, but it Was not supposed the members would come together for the despatch of business until January. was fought on the 28th of August, before the city of Lisbon, but without decided advantage to either party. MONEY þÿMARKETS CITY NEWS. New York Saturday, Oct. 14, p. m. The Orpheus, from Liverpool, brings lis dates down to the 16th of September. The political news is not of much importance. þÿ The Cotton market had fallen off' a little. In London there was more spirit in the market

The Cotton market at Liverpool in rather a depressed state, which had previously advanced, was falling off' a little, and the sales were quite limited for the week ending the 16th. There had been a fall on all descriptions of about jSjd. per lb. Colonial produce bad undergone no change. The money market had become so abundant that the Bank of England had reduced the rate of interest from five to four per cent. The bank had been forced to take this position, from the fact that the bankers loaned at three, and even as low as two and a half. The tardy and unwilling course of the bank in coming down to the passing rate of interest, had given great offence. English securities had all advanced, Consols up to 62. We think that we have never before seen them reach so high a point. Railway Stocks bon are to the 7th of September. A battle j have also nil gone up. Several vessels had reached England from America with specie, and among them the Westminster from New York, with a quarter of a million of dollars. A good feeling begins to be manifested, and the trade of America to be sought after. The fact is that the Americans have paid up so rapidly that they have astonished John Bull, A Liverpool paper announcing the arrival of the Oxford and Independence from this " port, says, The intelligence brought by these vessels is gratifying, and shows that the affairs of the United Stales are rapidly assuming a healthy and encouraging aspect. The Independence brought 200,000 dollars, and the

Oxford about 100,000. In faet the Americans have acted with promptitude aud integiity in discharging their pecuniary engagements with this country. For a considerable length ot time past, the amount of specie received at this port alone, from the United States, has averaged a million and a half of dollars per month, to say nothing of the remittances made during the same period in cotton and unexceptionable paper. The debt, therefore, due by America to Great Britain is rapidly in the course of liquidation, and the Americans, so far from deserving censure, are entitled to credit, for the energy and zeal which they have displayed intiie settlement oi our claims." Business all over England seems brightening in England. A Hull paper states that such is the briskness of the trade there, that the wages of common laborers have been raised from 3s to 3s 6d a day. The demand for labor is so great, that there need not at present be a single able-bodied man out of employ.

Destructive Storm at New Orleans. A violent storm and gale of wind did great damage in New Orleans and its neighbourhood, on the night of the 6th instant In the city, chimney tops were blown down, awnings ripped up, houses unroofed, dj c. The masts of several vessels were carried away, and many vessels at anchor went ashore. Two Steamboats drifted across the river, and were much injured. Considerable injury was done to the splendid new building, now in the process of erection for an Exchange. Several pillars and part of the front of the Citizen's Bank in Toulouse street were blown down. þÿ The Picayune, from which paper we gather these particular s, has the following additional statement. Great Destruction or Property ! ! þÿ Further Effects of the Storm ! for merchandise. Indigo had advanced. þÿ Just as our paper was going to press, a gentleman informed us that the destruction of property at the rail road on lake Pontchartrain by the storm has been very great. All the boats at the piers were completely wrecked, and driven into the woods, except the South Alabama. The steamers Merchant and Mobile, ( the two best boats in the trade,) and the Columbia and Pontchai train, are a total wreck, being so much injured as to be un fit for further use. The ivavcs are mountain high in the lake ' þÿ All the houses at the rait road were blown down except two The scene is one of distress and uncommon ruin. The water is three or fourfeet above the rail road. II e are pained to hear this news but cannot iiait to give the
particulars. The loss of property must be immense. Two hands on board the Columbia drowned ; several other lives lost. Particulars in our next.

MESSAGE FROM T1IR PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES To the two Houses of Congress at the commencement of the first session oj the Twentyfifth Congress. Fellow Citizens oj the Senate and House of Representatives : þÿ ( Concluded from our last.) It is tiue that the bank notes actually convertible into specie may be received in payment of the revenue, without being liable to all these objections, and that such a course may, to some extent, promote individual convenience ; an object always to be considered where it does not conflict with the principles of our Government or the general welfare of the country. If such notes only were received, and always under circumstances allowing the early presentation for payment, and if, at short and fixed periods, they were converted into specie, to be kept by the officers of the Treasury, some of the most serious obstacles to their reception would perhaps be removed. To retain the notes in the Treasury would be to renew, under another form, the loans of public money to the banks and the evils con sequent thereon. It is, however, a mistaken impression, that any large amount of specie is required for public payments. Of the seventy or eighty millions now estimated to be in the country, ten millions would be abundantly sufficient for that purpose, provided an accumulation of a large amount of revenue, beyond the necessary wants of the Government, be hereafter prevented. If to these considerations be added the facilities which will arise from ena-

bling the Treasury satisfy the public cre- to ditors, by its drafts or notes received in payment of the public dues, it may be safely assumed that no motive of convenience to the citizen requires the reception of bank paper. To say that the refusal of paper money by the governments introduces an unjust discri- j mination between the currency received by i it auii that used by individuals in their ordinary affair, is, in my judgment, to view it in a very erroneous light. The Constitution ! prohibits the States from making any thing | have interdicted their doubtless, but gold and silver a tender in the payment of debts, and thus secures to every citizen a right to demand payment in the legal currency. To provide by law that the Government will only receive its dues in gold and silver is not to confer on it any peculiar privilege ; but merely to place it on an equality with the citizen, but reserving to it a right secured to him by the Constitution. It is doubtless for this reason that the principle has been sanctioned by successive laws, from the time of the first Congress under the Constitution down to the last. Such precedents, never objected to and proceeding from much sources, afford a decisive answer to the imputation of inequality or injustice. But, in fact, the measure is one of restriction, not ol favor. Io forbid the public agent to receive in payment any other than a cer- j without doubt be tain kind of money, is to refuse him a discre- ! tion possessed by every citizen. It may be

left to those who have the management of their own transactions, to make their own terms, but no such discretion should be given to him who merely acts as an agent of the people, who is to' collect what the law and to pay the appropriations it makes. When bank

When they are not so redeemed, it will scarcely be contended ! that their receipt and payment, by a public officer, should be permitted, though none deny that right to an individual ; if it were the officer would be most injurious to the public, since their officer could make none ol those arrangements to meet or guard against the depreciation, which an individual is at liberty to do. Nor can inconvenience to the community be alledged as an objection to such regulation. Its object and motive are their convenience and welfare If, at a moment of simultaneous and unexpected suspension by the banks, it adds something to the many embarassmcnls of that proceeding, yet those are ovei balanced by its direct tendency to produce a wider circulation of gold and silver to increase the safety of bank paper, to improve the general currency, and thus to prevent altogether such occurrences, and the other and far greater evils that atteud them. it may, indeed, be questioned, whether it is not for the interest of the bai ks themselves that the government should not receive their paper. J hey would be conducted with more caution, and on sounder principles. By using specie only in its transactions, the government would create a demand for it, which would to a great extent, prevent its exportation, and

by keeping it in circulation, maintain a broader and safer basis for the paper currency. That the banks would thus be rendered more sound, and the community more safe, cannot admit of a doubt. J he foregoing views, it seems to me, do but fairly carry out the provisions of the Federal Constitution in relation to the currency, as far as relates to the the time that instrument was framed, there were but two or three banks in the United States ; and had the extension of the banking system, and the evils growing out of it been foreseen, they would probably have been speciaHy guarded against. The same policy which led to the prohibition of bills of credit by the Stales, would, in that event, j issue as a currency in any other form. The Constitution however, j contains no such prohibition ; and, since the i States have exercised for nearly half a century the power to regulate the business of bunk- I mg, it is not to be expected that it will be abandoned. Seeing that the immediate enforcement of these obligations would subject a large and highly respectable portion of our citizens to great sacrifices, and believing that a temporary postponement could be made without detriment to other interests, and with increased certainty of ultimate payment. Similar information is communicated in regard to such depositories of the public moneys as are indebted to the Government, or order that Congress may also adopt the proper measure in regard to them.

The receipts and expenditures for the first half ol the year, and an estimate of those for the residue, will be laid before you by the Secretary of the I reasury. In bis report of December last, it was estimated that tbe current receipts would fall short of the expenditures by about three millions of dollars. This þÿl awto he iccalled, if needed, to defray existing appropriations; and as it is now evident that the whole, or the principal part of if. will he wanted Jor that purpose, it appears most pro-

Relying upon the acts of Congress which held out to them the strong probability, if not the certainty, of receiving this instalment, they have in some instances adopted measures with which its retention may. seriously interfere. That such a condition of things should have occurred is much to be regretted. It is not the least among the unfortunate results of the disasters of the times ; and it is for Congress to devise a fit remedy, if there be one. The money being indispensable to the wants of the Treasury, it is difficult to perceive upon what principle of justice or expediency its application to that object can be avoided. To recall any portions of the sums already deposited with the States, would be more inconvenient and less efficient. To burden the country with increased taxation, when there is in fact a large surplus revenue, would be unjust and unwise ; to raise moneys by loans under such circumstances, and thus to commence a new national debt, would scarcely be sanctioned by the American people. The plan proposed will be adequate to all our fiscal operations, during the remainder of the year. Should it be adopted, the Treasury, aided by the am pile resources of the country, will he able to discharge punctually every pe-

cuniary obligation For the future, all that is needed will lie that caution and forbearance in appropriations which the diminution of the revenue requires, and which the complete accomplishment or great forwardness of many expensive national undertakings renders equally consistent with prudence and patriotic liberality. The preceding suggestions and recommendations are submitted, in the belief that their adoption by Congress will enable the Execu tive Department to conduct our fiscal concerns with success, so far as their management has been committed to it. Whilst the objects and the means proposed to attain them, are within its Constitutional powers and appropriate duties, they will at the same time, it is hoped ; by their necessary operation, afford essential aid in the transaction of individual concerns, and thus yield relief to the people at large in a form adapted to the nature of our Government. Those who look to the action of this Government for specific aid to the citizen to relieve embarrassments arising from losses by revulsions in commerce and credit, lose sight of the ends for which it was created, and the powers with which it is clothed It was established to give security to us all, in our lawful and honorable pursuits, under the lasting safeguard of republican institutions. It was not intended to confer special favors on individuals, or on any classes of them; to create systems of agriculture, manufacturers, or trade ; or to engage in them, either sepa-

vatively or in connection with individual citizens or organized associations. If its operations were to bo directed for the benefit of any one class, equivalent favors must, in justice, be extended to the rest, and tin; attempt to bestow such favors with au equal hand, or even to select those who should most deserve them, would never be successful. All communities are apt to look to Government for too much. Even in our own country, where its powers uud duties arc so strictly

The framers of our excellent Constitution, and the people who approved it with calm and sagacious deliberation, acted at the time on a sounder principle. They wisely judged that the less Go- i vernments interferes witli private pursuits, the better for the general prosperity. It is not its legitimate object to make men rich, or to repair, by direct grants of money or legislation in favor of particular pursuits, losses not incurred in the public service. This would be substantially to use the property of some for the benefit of others. Rut its real duty þÿ that duty, the performance of which makes a good Government the most precious of human blessings þÿ a system of general laws commensurate with, but not exceeding, the objects of its establishment, and to leave every citizen and every interest to reap, under its benign protection, the rewards of virtue, industry, and prudence. I cannot doubt that on this, as on all similar occasions, the Federal Government will 1 find its agency most conducive to the security and happiness of the people, when limited to the exercise of its conceded powers. In | never assuming, even for a well meant object, j tification to know, by long experience, that such powers as were not designed to be conferred upon it, we shall in reality do most for the general welfare. To avoid every unnecessary interference with the pursuits of the

citizen, will result in more benefit than to adopt measures which could only assist limited interests, and are eagerly, but perhaps naturally, sought for, under the pressure of temporary circumstances. If, therefore, I refrain from suggesting to Congress any specific plan for regulating the exchanges of the country ; relieving mercantile embarrassments; or interfering with the ordinary operations of foreign or domestic commerce ; it is from a conviction that such measures are not within the constitutional province of the General Government, and that their adoption would not j promote the real and permanent welfare of those they might be designed to add. The ditficulties and distresses of the times, though unquestionably great, are limited in their extent, and cannot be regarded as affecting the permanent prosperity of the nation, j which the Constitution requires me to <_rive. Arising, in a great degree, from the transactions of foreign and domestic commerce, it is upon them that they have chiefly fallen. The groa. agricultural interest has, in many parts of the country, suffered comparatively little ; and, as if þÿI rovidence intended to display the munificence of its goodness at the moment of our greatest need, and in direct contrast to the evils occasioned by the waywardness of man, we have been blessed throughout our extended territory with a season of general health and of uncommon fruitfulness. abroad, and contribute equally to tho revival of commercial activity, and the restoration of commercial credit. The suspension of specie payments, at such a time and under such circumstances as we have lately witnessed, could not be other than a temporary measure ; we can scarcely err in believing that the period must soon arrive when all that are solvent will redeem their issues in gold and silver. It is now about two months since an agency of the British Colonial Rank commenced its operations in this town, under the direction of James Brown, Esq. and it is with satisfaction we announce that they have hitherto been of great service to the Proprietors and other inhabitants of the Island, by loaning out sums at legal interest, thereby enabling many to pay in their tares due to >h» Royal Government, which must otherwise have laid over ; also by furnishing such sums as are required to carry the pioprietors into the new crop, and facilitating remittances to St. Thomas and the. neighboring Islands. The well known solidity of this institution, its ex. tensive, capital, the high-standing of the Hirectoi s in London, and the respectability of its agents in the J 1 'est Indies, alt combine to render it a useful institution, in which every confidence may be placed þÿ we sincerely hope that success will attend its establishment , and induce its continuance in the Island þÿ we are happy to add that its bills are freely taken at all the Government Offices, in payment for dues ; þÿ they are at all times redeemable in specie.

Though much has been done during the parental Administration of Earl Mulgravc to heal the wounds which the avarice, and despotism, and fanaticism of monopoly had deeply þÿinflicted (hough that beloved and unequalled Viceroy can boast as standing at the head of the most enthusiastically loyal portion of the Briti.sii Empire at the present moment though he can, for the first time in the history of British connection with Ireland, command the hearts and hands of millions of as brave and a Lie men as Europe could produce though stieh is the just return for the protection Earl Mulgrave aflords to all men of all denominations; yet what blessing has that most excellent Nobleman conferred on Ireland compared to the promised blessing of a legal refuge for Iter destitute suffering and patient poor. rfth, or destroy the person and property of his neighbour þÿ for the first time an attempt is made by the Legislature to raise up the great body of the people from the most indescribable degree of misery, and to place Ireland in the list of civilized nations which make the demands ofthe destitute poor the most imperative obligation of the community. Your Petitioner begs leave to join his countrymen in the expression ot their gratitude lor extending to Ireland the protecting prinple of a Poor-law ; and however he may lament that in the carrying into effect that principle your Petitioner does not see that confidence which should ever he reposed in the understanding and good feeling of his countrymen, yet with all the objections which have been and winch may be justly urged against the machinery of the Bill now in progress, yet your Petitioner thanks your Honourable House for making a beginning, and for the first time striking a blow at that selfish, cruel, and heartless spirit, which lias too long distinguished the proprietors of land in Ireland, who, with a few exceptions, have ever been the enemies of every arrangement which would make their properly responsible to any extent for the wants of the poor þÿ of that very poor whose labor enriched that property and enabled its possessors to waste it in foreign countries to the ruin and disgrace of their own. A reformed House of Commons, to its immortal honour, has grappled with this principle of selfishness and has at length vindicated

the claims of the most patient and forbearing peasantry the world now presents to human sympathy. Your Petitioner begs leave to state that the Catholic Hierarchy of Ireland, in solemn synod, have supplicated your Honourable House to enact a Poor-law for Ireland ; that the metropolis of Ireland, assembled under the auspices and presidency of the Lord Mayor of Dublin, have sent forward the same prayer ; and that the great majority (your petitioner might say all the Catholic Clergy of Ireland) will respond to the same feeling. Your petitioner has struggled hard for a series of years to raise his Protestant countrymen to the same platform of freedom on which the Protestant stood so long without a competitor. But though the attainment of that great national good should call forth his gratitude to all those who joined in accomplishing it, yet your Petitioner has ever considered the emancipation of the Irish peasantry from their present unutterable state of destitution, as by far the greatest blessing a wise and beneficent Government could confer. Differing as your Petitioner often has differed on this great question from some of the most practically useful and deservedly admired friends Ireland ever had, yet lie has the consolation to reflect that he is sustained in this opinion by the high authorities he has quoted þÿ by the wisdom and parental feeling of a reformed House of Commons þÿ and by the thoughtful, well and laboriously considered determination of the present Irish Govern-

ment, which has based its powers on the af- Icc -ns ol tile Irish people : and true to its professions, multiplies by the days which pass over it, its claims on its confidence and its immortal title to national gratitude. our Petitioner, therefore, humbly prays your honourable House to go on with the Irish Boor-law Bill, which in a few years will bo better known as the Irish Poor Man's Charter. And your Petitioner will ever pray, John Lawless. London, June 5.

If there be any thing connected with mercantile business woilhy of admiration and calculated to elevate the moral character of American merchants, it is the unremitting and energetic exertions of those in the Atlantic cities to pay their just debts. With hut little thus far to encourage and much to unnerve, they seem resolved that lliey can pay and will pay, regardless of sacrifices For the past twelve months exchanges have been constantly growing worse, and as a consequence payments by those at a distance have been much interrupted and delayed. Duty and interest both call upon the country merchants to strain every nerve in aid of their city friends, and it should now more than ever he their pride to offer every facility to those who have been so long struggling against odds. This course determined and acted upon coupled with a refusal to make new engagements beyond necessity, will soon relieve

the whole trading community, and restore business to its former healthy and invigorated condition. A sacrifice of profit should deter none from meeting their engagements : none now should despair, for with energy and perseverance brighter days will break upon the mercantile community as certainly as that the fields which hut a short time since seemed to deny every thing are now offering abundance. The present liabilities of the whole country, as compared with the corresponding period of last year, are supposed not much to exceed one half, and a few are disposed to add to them. Let the farmer seek an early market for their produce and with the proceeds pay the country merchants. The latter will then be enabled to appear in the cities, and by doing the best they can, should they fall short of their meeting their engagements, their presence alone will afford encouragement and strengthen their friends on the seaboard. These suggestions in all probability have already been anticipated ; in one instance, which lias come to our knowledge, they certainly have been acted out in a praise worthy manner þÿ we allude to the recent arrival here of a gentleman from a South western State, who has established himself in this city for the purpose of receiving the cotton of sundry planters and merchants, and paying their lia bilities with the proceeds. A few "such instances will aid greatly in restoring confidence. þÿ Baltimore American.

From the St. Christopher Gazette, Oct. 5. An awful or.curienoe took place on Sunday morning last, which had it happened with the night time, may have been attended in serious consequences. At an early hour on that morning, distant peals of thunder were heard, unaccompanied at that time by any lightning but between t> and 7 o'clock, the þÿ thunder became very appalfng with vivid flashes of lightning, the former being instantaneous with the latter, their descent being very near the earth. At about quarter past 7 o'clock, a terrific peal of thunder was heard and the lightning struck a House (occupied) in Pall Mall Square, the property of Mr. John IJerkelv, adjoining his residence, and materially injured it It appears to have gone through the roof, splitting several rafters, and went through a window shutter and descended in the earth. A servant of Mr Berkeley's perceiving a sulphuerous smell, and smoke issuing from the window, gave the alarm, and the flame was quickly subdued by water being thrown on it. Thanks to Divine Providence that this occurrence took place in the day time, as it may otherwise not have been so quickly discovered, and extinguished, and a part of the Town may have been destroyed.

(From the Railway Magazine for July!) On Thursday evening the 8th June, a very interesting Lecture was delivered by Mr. Zincke at the Adelnid Gallery, on the Fibre of the Pine Apple Leaf, which promises to be of considerable value in a commercial and manufacturing point of view, Mr Lister, the Microscopist, has minutely examined this fibre, and has observed that it is a fascicuious or bundle of ultimate fibres, united together by a membrane or a gummy matter. þÿ The diameter of an ultimate fibre of pine is found to vary from 1 -3000th to l-7000th of an inch, while the fibre of flax varies from l-700th to 1 -'2500th. It has also been observed that the fibre of flax is interrupted by joints, while that ol line lias the advantage of been a conlinous cylinder. Silk is likewise perfectly cylindrical, and varies from l-1500tli to 1-I700th of an inch in diameter, and a Cotton fibre is a flattened and twisted cylinder, its diameter varying from about 1 700lh to 1- 100th of an inch. It will be seen that the pine fibre far exceeds the oilier thread in fineness, and Mr. Zincke assured the audience that the operation of separating these fibres from the fasciculus, and destroying the unnecessary matter, is simple in the extreme. And experiment was tried on the comparative strength of flax and pine ; 7 J ounces were sufficient to break a thread ot the former, while 8j, ounces were required to break a thread of the latter. One most valuable quality is possessed by the pine fibre, and that is, its capability of receiving and re-

taining dye, while coloring matter invariable peels of flax. The cost of rearing this plant in the West Indies (no idea is entertained of making it an English article) is so very small, that, the fibre could be delivered in England at the expense of 4 I per pound ol course exclusive of duty, while from two to three acres of land are sufficient to yield a Ton of the fibre.

cur'. for hydrophobia. In various parts of South America this dreadful disease is extremely common in the violent heats of summer. The wild beasts in a country but ill supplied with streams, and in the long summer when those springs are diied np, tear their flesh in agony with this disease. The wolves and all the dog kind are the especial sufferers but the jaguars, or tigers, and perhaps all that roam the sandy plains, are seized willi this fury. Accidents are of course common among the hunters, herdsmen, and the people ol the lower ranks in general ; but they excite comparatively little terror, from the frequency and simplicity of the cure. This is effected by taking two or three doses of a powdered root, which seems something of a helebore genus, and of which Lieutenant Hardy gives the characters. The root throws the patient into the most profuse perspiration ; the second day generally completes the cure, though ,the patient remains weak for a time. It is remarkable that this root acts in the same manner as the only medicines which have been found a palliative of this dreadful disease in Europe. Sudorilies alone seem to have produced any effect here, and some instances of the singular force of the vapour hath in quieting the paroxysms have been given within these few years, which may tend to a more skilful treatment. All this, however, has been told to our English surgeons already. The root

iffc-ciwwy . in questions has even been brought to England and administered, but, as is reported, without effect. Still we know how hard it is to convince any man, even an hospital surgeon, against his will, what slight circumstances may he taken advantage of. and what important ones may be neglected, where the mind of the experimentalist is not in favour of the operation ; we must suspend our belief that the root, which had so plainly wrought its cure in South America, becomes utterly useless on crossing the Atlantic. The man who shall succeed in bringing hydrophobia within the power of European medicine will deserve the highest gratitude of Europe, and | will doubtless leceive the most valuable testimonials of the liberality ol England. þÿ Blackwood,

When William Penn was about to sail from England to Pennsylvania, lie went to take leave of the King, and the following conversation occurred " Well, friend William," said Charles, " 1 have sold you a noble province in North America, hut still I suppose you have no thoughts of going thither yourself" "Yes 1 have," replied William, "and I am just come to bid thee farewell." " What! venture yourself among the savage of North America ' Why, man, what security have you that you will not be in their wash-kettle in two hours after setting foot on their shores?" " The best security in the world," replied Penn. " I doubt that, my friend William; I have no idea of any security against those cannibals but in a regiment of good soldiers with their muskets and bayonets ; and mind I tell you before hand, that with all my good will for you and your family, to whom I am under obligations, 1 will not send a single soldier with you." " 1 want none of thy soldiers," answered William, " I depend on something better than thy soldiers " The K ing wished to know what that was " Why, 1 depend on themselves þÿ on their own moral sense þÿ even that grace ofGod, which bringeth salvation, and which hath appeared unto all men." " I fear, friend Will iam, that that grace has never appeared to the Indians of North America." " Why not to them as well as to others ?" " If it had appeared to them,1' said the King, ' they would hardlv have treated my subjects so barbarously as they have done." " That is no proof to the contrary,

lrieud Charles. Thy subjects were the aggressors. When thy subjects first went to North America, they found these people the fondest and kindest creatures in the world. Every day they would watch for them to conic on shore, and hasten to meet them, and feast them on their best fish and venison and corn, which was ali they had. In reiurn for the hospitality of the savages, as we call them, thy subjects, termed Christians, seized on their country, and rich hunting grounds, or farms, for themselves ! Now, is it to be wondered at that these much-injured people should have been driven to desperation by such injustice . and that, burning with revenge, they should have committed some excesses ?" " Well, then, I hope, friend Wiiliam, you will not complain when they come to treat you in the same manner." « 1 am not afraid of it," said Penn. " Aye ! how will you avoid it? You mean to get their hunting-grounds, too, I suppose ?" ' Yes, but not by driving these poor people away from them." " No, indeed, how then will you get their lands?" " 1 mean to buy their lands of them." » Buy their lands of them! Why, man, you have already bought them of þÿme." Yes, " I know I have, and at a dear rate too ; but I did it only to get thy good- will, not that I thought thou hadst any right to their lands. No, friend Charles, no right at all ; what right hadst thou to their lands ! ' ' Why, the right of discovery ; the right which the Pope and all Christian Kings have agreed to give one another." " The

right of discovery ! A strange kind of right, indeed. Now suppose, friend Charles, some canoe-loads of those Indians, crossing the sea, and discovering thy Island of Great Britain, were to claim it as their own, and set it for sale over thy bond, what would'st thou think Charles, I must confess 1 should think a a of them?" " " þÿWhy why why." replied

Well, then, how canst thou a Christian, and a Christian prince, too, do that which thou utterly condemnest in these people whom thou callest savages? Yes If iend Charles, and suppose again that those Indians, on thy refusal to give up thy islands of Great Britain, were to make war on thee, and having weapons more destructive than thine, were to destroy many of thv subjects, and to drive the rest away, do'st thou not think it horribly cruel ?" The King assented to this with marks of conviction. William proceeded: " Well, then, friend Charles, how can 1, who call myself a Christian, do that which 1 should abhor in an heathen ? No, I will not do it þÿ but I will buy the right of the proper owners, even of the Indians themselves. By doing this, 1 shall imitate God himself in his justice and mercy and thereby ensure his blessing on my colony, if 1 should ever live to plant one in North America." þÿ Pennsylvania soon became a flourishing colony, and existed for seventy years, (the period when the quakers held the Government,) without any force beyond that of the constable's staff þÿ and during that seventy years it was never invaded by hostile power from land or sea. þÿ Weem's Life of William l'ena.

WOMAN'S LOVE. I never heard Of any true ahection, but 'twas nipt With care that, like the caterpillar, cats 'i lie leaves ol the Spring's sweetest hook, the rose. Middletoiv. It is a common practice with those who have outlived the susceptibility of early feeling, or have been brought up in the gay heartlessness of dissipated file, to laugh at all love stories, and to treat the talcs ol romatr tic passion as mere fictions of novelists and poets. Mv observations on human naiurc have induced me to think otherwise. They have convinced me that however the surface of the character may bo chilled and frozen !>v the cares of the world, or cultivated into mere smiles by the arts of society, still there are dormant fires lurking in the depths of the coldest bosoms, which, when once enkindled, become impetuous, and are soirelimes desolating in their effects. Indeed 1 am a true believer, in the blind deity, and go to the full

I believe in broken hearts, and the possibility of dying of disappointed love 1 I do not, however, consider, it a malady often fatal to my own sex ; but 1 firmly believe that it withers down many a lovely woman to an early grave. Man is the creature of interest and ambition. His nature leads him forth into the struggle and bustle of the world. Love is but the embellishment of his carlv life, or a song piped at the intervals of the acts. He seeks for fame, lor fortune, lor space in the world's thought, and dominion over his fellow men ; but a woman's whole life is a history ol the alleolions. The heart is her world it ; is there her ambition strives for empire ; it is there her avarice seeks for hidden treasures. She sends forth her sympathies on adventure; she embarks her whole soul in the trullic of affection ; and il shipwrecked, her case is þÿhopeless for it is a bankruptcy of the heart. To a man the disappointment of love may occasion some bitter pangs ; it wounds some leeling oi þÿtenderness it blasts some prospeets

of felicity ; hut he is an active being þÿ he Can dissipate his thoughts in the whirl of varied occupation, or plunge into the tide of pleasure; or, if the scene of disappointment be too full of painful associations, he can shift his abode at will, and, taking as it were the wings of the morning, can fly to the uttermost parts of the earth, and he at rest. But woman's is comparatively a fixed, a secluded, and a meditative life. She is more the companion of her own thoughts and feelings; and if they are turned to ministers of sorrow, where shall she look for consolation ; Her lot is to be woed and won ; and if uuhappy in her love, her heart is like some fortress that has been captured, and sacked, and abandoned, arid left desolate. How many bright eyes grow dim þÿ how many soft cheeks grow pale þÿ how many lovely forms fade away into the tomb, at d none can tell the cause that blighted their loveliness ! As the dove will clasp its wings to its side, and cover and conceal the arrow that is preying on its vitals, so it is the nature of woman to hide from the world the pangs of wounded atfection. The love of a delicate female is always shy and silent. Even when fortunate she scarcely breaths it to herself: t ut when otherwise, she buries it in the recesses of her bosom, and there lets it cower and brood among the ruins of her peace. With her the desire of the heart has failed. The great charm of existence is at an < ml She neglects all the cheerful exercises which glad-

Queen Victoria made her first visit to Windsor, since her accession to the throne, on the 25th Aug þÿ It was a great gala-day at Windsor, where extensive preparations, fire- works, baloon ascensions, &c. awaited her þÿ tables were spread for 4,000 people in the open air, and that number of the poorer classes regaled themselves with a good dinner; but unfortunately a heavy fall of rain took place while they were seated at the tables, which were soon hid by the Umbrellas, from under which, the viands quickly disappeared þÿ the young Queen was in an open carriage, exposed to the rain, with merely an Umbrella held over, þÿ she appeared highly gratified, bowed graciously to the great concourse which accompanied her, and we are happy to add her Majesty experienced no inconvenience from the inclemency of the weather. Mrs Graham, the lady who fell from the baloon some time since, made another ascension on the above occasion.

From the Barbadian, Sept. 23, The only topic þÿ and it ought to be a very serious one with all of us, þÿ of conversation to day is, the Earthquake of the last evening. This alarming convulsion of the earth occurred about a quarter after seven o'clock. In the house in which we reside we felt three distinct vibrations. The siiock appeared to us to be slight, and to have continued not more than live seconds. In other parts of the town, however, particularly the Bier, and in houses near the Wharf, and in Broad street, the shock was most alarmingly violent, and must have continued at least 15 seconds þÿ .Several persons were dreadfully terrified by the violent shaking of the houses, and furniture and the clattering of the glass windows. We did not ourselves perceive the direction of it ; but several persons who felt the motion more perceptibly, remark that the undulations were from N. to S. It was altogether an awful looking night, the heavens black, and vivid flashes of lightning, with heavy rains, and at times the wind extremely fresh from the E. and S. E. At eleven o'clock the wind rose to such an alarming height as to rouse ome families from their beds, but a calm very suddenly followed, and the remainder of the night was quiet with frequent rain. The morning at 5 þÿo clock was fine, and the air had a delicious coolness. Above Two Mile Hill we saw the sun rising with a cheering brightness ; but he was soon obscured by thick clouds, and þÿw e have had much rain since. þÿ The weather looks very unsettled at this mo-

ment (11 þÿo clock) þÿ not an unusual circumstance at the period of the .Sun crossing the line. Equinoctial gales are very likely to occur, particularly in the Western Ocean. May God be gracious to us in this trying season ! It has been many years since we have been visited with Earthquakes, in this Island, of a very alarming nature. The last severe shock was on the 22d December 1810, when the large house in Broad street, opening on the waterside, then in the possession of Mr. Francis Williams (now Messrs Halv's, was split from top to bottom ; and it is very remarkable that this very house was injured by the Earthquake of last evening. We understand that every wall of the building is cracked. The house in the same street also, occupied by Mr. Andeuson, (Watchmaker,) is so much injured as to be considered very unsafe. We have not yet heard from manv of the Parishes, but are informed that the sho. k was sensibly felt in St. Philip's Christ Church, and St. George's, at Black Rock and at Hastings. þÿ Tlie voice of God has indeed spoken to us within the last two months, in the Wind, in the Fire and in the Earthquake. Shall not þÿ the still, small þÿvoice of conscience speak to us of the past, warn us of the future, and tell us to use the present moment to prepare for other, perhaps more awful changes ? Shall it not remind us of the words of Inspiration, that to the truly penitent, the God who put that secret moniter into our hearts, is a þÿ God of þÿmercy, but to the impenitent, a þÿ

consuming þÿfire ? Our friends who think seriously will excuse our moralising on the present occasion. We cannot let these awful dispensations our Maker pass withonl ex- of pressing those feelings which they always rouse in our mind. Fallible man is apt to attribute the various phenomena which frequently alarm us to the mere operation of second cause ; but if there is a second cause it irresistibly compel us to

New Printing Press. One of our most ingenious mechanics, Mr Ihomas French, has invented a new J tinting i rcss, which will eclipse every thing of the kind heretofore put in operation. It is intended for stereotype plates, and will work ofT fifty reams of paper, of mammoth size, per day. It is intended to be attached to paper mills, and will print as fast as any mill can manufacture, without any other help than that required to manufacture the paper. The register, by a simple regulation, can easily be changed, and made perfect. We have now n sheet in our office worked on this new press, 2<! feet long, printed on both sides at a time, in a quartor of a minute. The sheet contains two book of 160 pages eac.h. I he cost of a first rate press, on this principle, will not exceed 1000 dollars.

One of the Wonders of the. þÿAge. We have been shewn a sheet of paper about one hundred feet in length, aud two feet wide, printed on both sides by a machine at one operation. This extraordinary invention enables a poison to print off any length of paper required for any number of copies of a work or a public journal, without a single stop, and without the assistance of any person except one to put in the rags at the extremity of the machine. The work Comes out entire and complete. This wonderful operation is effected by the placing of the types on stereotype plates on the surface of two cylinders, which are connected with the paper making machinery. The paper, ns it issues from the mill, enters in a properly moistened state between the rollers, which are evenly inked by an ingenious apparatus, and emerges in a printed form. The number of copies can be measured ofF by the yard or mile, according to the demand, or according to the supply of the þÿ raw þÿmaterial. The work which we have seen from this press is þÿ Robinson Cruþÿsoe, and consists of one hundred and sixty duodecimo pages. All that is necessary for a man to do on going into a paper mill, is to take olFhis shirt, hand it to the devil who officiates at one extremity, and have it come out Robinson Crusoe at the other. Mr. Thomas French, of Utica, is the inventor. þÿ American Sun .

St. Croix, CHRISTIAN STED, (MON DA Y) October 23, 1837. (COMMUNICATION.) The. period having nearly approached when the Hurricane season usually terminates in tropical latitudes, we are naturally led to reflect upon the advantages our favored Island has enjoyed over our neighbors , not only during the present season, but for many years bach, in having been touch less frequently visited with these dreadful scourges or in feeling them in a much slighter degree than any of the other Islands, þÿ whether this advantage is owing to our being placed out of the semicircular tine of the other Islands, or. from other causes, we know not ; perhaps the same cause which makes us more subject to long droughts than our neighbors, may produce both our exemption from frequent hurricanes (or our feeling them in a much milder degree) and also our long droughts. þÿ Certain, however it is, that the present season we have been remarkably favored ; þÿ The hurricane of the 2d August was experienced here in a very slight degree, and the carnage incurred was trifling when compared witii that of our neighbors ; þÿ and this is the more remaikable considering our proximity to St. Thomas ( only forty miles distant), and to Tortola. St. John's and Porto Rico, in alt which Islands, heavy losses were experienced : þÿ and Islands hundreds of miles from us, also suffered severely, as witness St. Martins, St. Barts, St Kitts, Antigua <$ Nevis; þÿ whereas the hurricane of the 2d August was to us rather an advantage than otherwise, from the rains which then fell,

and which the Island greatly needed at that period. When we look back to the parched and dry state of our Island in June last, the miserable \ prospect which then existed for the coming crop, and compare that period with the one we have now reached, the verdant and luxuriant appearance of vegitation which now surrounds us, how much reason have we to be grateful to the great Giver of all. good for His bounty towards us þÿl If gratitude is due from \ man to man for favors received, how much more is it due from man to the great Author of his being, to the Creator o f the Universe, and of all that þÿ live, and move and have their being l" þÿ and how can this feeling be better evinced by man, than by his doing all in his power to relieve the. unfortunate, and the distressed, the poor and the needy, the widow þÿ þÿ ! and the fatherless." þÿ to do this in an ostentatious, public display. þÿ i Christian charity should not court worldly applause; everyone in his own circle must find objects of charily around him who he. is bound to relieve, it he has the means, þÿ and moie particularly is this first anil greatest Christian virtue to be exercised towards those who are placed under us, and by þÿ the. sweat of whose brows' þÿ and by whose labor we enjoy the good things of this þÿworld, we should then do all in our power to alleviate their state ;

jdabtss: TJsstmrossjE uoiamos to discountenance oppression and injustice towards them þÿ to treat them as fellow beings, who possess the same affections and sympathies, the same sense of oppression and injustice as ourselves; and if our pecuniary interests should suffer by the exercise of that þÿ love to our neighbor þÿ winch is no mure than, our duty, why we may have the satisfaction to reflect that we are laying up treasures in Heaven, þÿ where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, nor thieves break through <£ steal."

From the Guiana Chronicle, Aug. 2. His Excellency the Governor, who yesterday ordered the discharge of seventy-two guns, as a tribute of respect to the memory of the defunct King, has delayed the proclamation of the Queen's accession until the arrival of official despatches. This is an anomalous procedure, unlike what we should have expected from an old soldier. The Colony is at this moment subject to no Sovereign. Surely the intelligence, if good for the announcement of one event, was good also for the celebration of the ceremony consequent on the oilier. Did his Excellence wish to keep the door open for the possible issue of the Dowager Queen ? By the charier of appointment of the Hereditary Lord High Chamberlain of England, he has the right to the dress worn hv the Soverign at each coronation, in which he is to appear on the first Court after that august ceremony. Those only who arc aware of the masses of papers submitted to the Sovereign, and the innumerable subjects on which his pleasure is necessarily taken, can appreciate the promptness, courtesy, and decision displayed by our late monarch. When the King went to the House of Lords to open the Parliament, the people marked their loyalty to his person by the loudest acclamations, but a different spirit was displayed towards his ministers. VVe have been informed of a singular circumstance in the history of Astronomical phenomena. A gentleman, who is in the habit of taking astronomical observations, tells us, that all the Primary Planets will have been in conjunction with the Moon between the 1st and the 17th of this month Whether these unusual motions of the Planets be indithis dreaded season, we leave it to during cative of any extraordinary weather philosolosophy tells us, that we are in the hands of phers to puzzle their brains about. Our phithe great and merciful Ruler of all those agents in the world of nature, and that they cannot move one step from their orbits without his will.

The conjunction of six of the primary planets with the moon in 17 days during this month, is no doubt a Phcenomenon in Astronomy of very rare occurrence, but there is not, we should imagine any thing in this circumstance at which Superstition even may terrify itself with imaginary fears. By the word conjunction, as applied to the Planets in the present instance we are to understand, that it can only occur when a superior planet is on the same side of the Sun, with the Earth, but in opposition to the Sun. These planets in moving round the Sun will sometimes when they are at the superior conjunctions be hid behind Inm and Venus and will then pass behind Mercury so that should the Moon be also in conjunction at the precise time, they will appear to have similar places in the heavens, with that planet. These conjunctions frequently happen unperceived and perhaps unknown even to astronomers : þÿ Mercury and the Moon were in conjunction on the 1st, at 9 minutes past 4 p. M. ; Jupiter on the 2nd, at 29 minutes past 1 p.m. j Venus on the 3d, at 2 minutes past 4 a. m. ; Mars on the 6th, at 14 minutes past 5 a.m. ; Saturn and the Moon will also lie in conjunction on the 9th at 9 minutes past 1 a.m ; and Herchel on the 17th, at 43 minutes past 9 p.m. ; besides which Mercury was in conjunction with Jupiter on the 7th, at 10 minutes past 5 f.m., Barbados time. þÿ Barbados Mercury Aug. 8.
