3BAST33R From the. Barbados Mercury, Sept. 2, 1837. By her Majesty's packet Pigeon 27 days from Falmouth, with the 1st August mails, we have received London journals to above date. These papers are almost wholly engrossed in furnishing particular statements of the progress or result of the elections for members to serve in the new House of Commons. The excitement appears to have been as lively and as general throughout the United lvingdon as it ever was perhaps, upon any former occasion of the kind According to a statement of the gain or loss of Conservative members, as compared with the last Parliament, the gain is given at 34, and the loss at 32 : thus it would seem as far as numbers will go, that the cause is prosperously progressing. Her Majesty prorogued Parliament in person, on Monday the 1 7th of last month But going to the House and returning from it, the Queen was followed by an immense crowd, crying out "God save the Queen- God bless Queen Victoria." Her Majesty, we find it mentioned, delivered the address in a very firm voice þÿ a circumstance which drew forth general remark, consiuering her tender age.

PROROGATION OF PARLIAMENT. HOUSE of þÿlords MONO AY, JUT Y 17. The house presented a most animated nppearance, not a single seat was unoccupied. Below the bar, the space appropriated for peers sons þÿ very limited in extent, certainly was crowded. In the gallery not a seat was unoccupied, and in the side galleries a great many ladies were imterspersed with peers. Every portion of the interior of the house was completely filled. Peers, indeed, were sitting so close together that they must have felt a little inconvenience, and others stood, unable to find seats at all. The number of peers who had assembled by two o'clock amounted to about 120. To enumerate them would be to give the names of all those who are conspicuous as politicians. he whole of the ambassadors were present. The Duchess of Kent entered the house a few minutes after two and took her seat oppositc the throne, and fronting it, a little inciining to the right. By her side was seated the Princess Leiningen, and, not distant from them, Lady Mary Stopford. At twenty minutes past two, salvoes of artillery and a flourish of trumpets, announced that her Majesty had arrived at the outer ! doors of the house. A rather unusual delay took place in the robing room ; and the Duchess of Kent more than once looked towards the entrance door very earnestly, and was engaged in conversation with the Duke of Sussex, who was near her, probably upon the cause of this delay. At length another flourish of trumpets was again heard, and in a few seconds the

heralds entered the house. ARRIVAL OF THE Qt'EEi. The joida in waiting succeeded the heralds, followed by the Duke of Norfolk with his' wand of office, as earl marshall, the great lord chamberlain, the Marquis of Lansdowne, the lord chancellor, the Marquis of YVincester, beating the cap of maintenance, Viscount Melbourne the sword of state, and the Duke of Somerset, with the crown imperial on a

JOfc'JtamaiTSIS AT3I3 crimson velvet cushion. Then came the Queen, attended by the Marchioness of Lansdowne and the Duchess of Sunderland, bearing her train, and followed by the Countess of Mulgrave as the lady in waiting. Her Majesty, having ascended the steps of the throne, immediately took her "seat, being surrounded by the great officers of state. The Queen was attired in a white satin dress, over which the royal robes were grace, fully thrown. She wore a crown of diamonds, said to have been the same worn by Queen Anne. She had on a magnificent stomacher of diamonds, as well as a splendid diamond necklace and ear rings ; the riband of the garter was conspicuous over her shoulder, It is impossible to conceive any one more at ease. Her sell possession struck all who beheld her. After a pause of a minute or two, the peers and peeresses having all risen on her ariival, her Majesty was pleased to request that jtlie peers would be seated. This direction was given in an unembarrassed, though rather feeble manner. The peers and peeresses then resumed their seats. bir Augustus Clifford, the usher of the black rod, kneeling at the foot of the steps of the throne, then received her Majesty's commands to summon the members of the commons. The Speaker, with a large number of members appeared at the bar in the course of a short time ; upon taking his station he addressed the Queen in the following words:-the speaker's address. " May it please your Majesty. YY e, your Majesty's faithful commons, at-

tend you on this, the first occasion, since your Majesty's accession to the throne of this united kingdom. " YVe assure your Majesty that we cordially participate in the strong and universal feeling of cordial and affectionate attachment to your Majesty's person, which prevails among all classes of the free and enlightened people, whose representatives we are ; and we trust that this feeling will be strengthened and confirmed by a long course of constitutional and beneficent and wise government. " Several bills, and one of them especially of the greatest diliiculty and importance, were recommended to our serious and deliberate consideration in the speech which was delivered by the lords commissioners on the part of his late Majesty at the opening of the present session of parliament. Circumstances have rendered it impossible that those measures should be perfected in the course of the present session. But we cherish the hope that the care and labour bestowed on them will not be in vain but will lead tbeir being hereafter matured and carried into cflect, with the general concurrence and assured prospect of promoting the welfare and happiness of the people. "We have passed an act for establishing, simplifying, and defining the law relating to the execution of wills. YVe confidently anticipate that this measure will be found to be most beneficial, because it tends to promote concord and happiness among a large portion of the community. I he mitigation and improvement of the

criminal law have engaged our most serious consideration, and we have materially diminished the number of cases in which capital punishment is to be inflicted. In framing those measures wc had the benefit of experi-

ence, which has shown that those punishments are incompatible with the enlightened state of the age ; that they carry with them a large portion of sympathy and feeling for the sufferers; and we cordially rejoice that we'bave been so far enabled to carry wise and humane principles of criminal legislation, which have been generally approved into effect. " YVe confidently anticipate that the efforts wc have made to mitigate the severity of the criminal law will this day receive the sanction of your Majesty's consent ; and hereafter the judgement of an enlightened and grateful people. " We have provided for the expenditure of this year with a strong regard to economy, and with a liberality which, we trust, will secure the efficiency of the public service, and enable your Majesty to maintain the dignity and honour of the crown. " YY'e now dutifully offer to your Majesty an act for the application of the sum of 5,220,0001. out of the consolidated fund for the service of the year 1837, and to appropriate the supplies granted in this session of parliament ; and we humbly pray your Majesty to give your royal assent thereto." The royal assent was then given to a number of bills with the accustomed formalities. HER MAJESTY'S SPEECH. The Queen then received from the lord chancellor the manuscript copy of the speech, which she proceeded to read. Nothing could exceed the accuracy of delivery, every emphatic word was distinctly marked ; and the euphonious tone ofher voice, which, although

somewhat of a youthful character, heightened the general effect. Persons in the most distant part of the house caught every syllable which she uttered, so clear and so distinct was her enunciation. " My Lords and Gentlemen, I have been anxious to seize the first opportunity of meeting you, in order that 1 might repeat in person my cordial thanks for your condolence upon the death of his late Majesty, and for the expressions of attachment and aflection with which you congrutulated me upon my accession to the throne. I am desirous of renewing the assurance «f my determination to maintain the protectant religion as established by law, to secure to all the free exercise of the rights of conscience, to piotect the liberties, and to promote the welfare ol all classes of the community. I rejoice that in ascending the throne I find the country in amity with all foreign powers ; and while I faithfully perform the engagements of my crown, and carefully watch over the interests of my subjects, it shall be the constant object of my solicitude to preserve the blessings of peace. " I thank you for the liberal "Gentlemen of the House of Commons. supplies which you have granted for the public service of the year, as well as for the provision which you have made to meet the payments usually chargeable upon the civil fist. " I will give directions that the public expenditure in all its branches be administered with the strictest economy. " In taking leave of this Gentlemen, iYly Lords, and parliament I return

you my thanks for the zeal and assiduity with which you have applied yourself to the public business of the country. " Although your labours have been unexpectedly interrupted by the melancholy event which has taken place, I trust that they will

have the beneficial effect of advancing the progress of legislation in a new parliament. 1 perceive with satisfaction that you have brought to maturity some useful measures, amongst which I regard, with peculiar interest, the amendment of the criminal code and the reduction of the number of capital punishments. I hail this mitigation of the severity of the law as an auspicious commencement of my reign. " I ascend the throne under a deep sense of the responsibility which is imposed upon nie ; but I am supported by the consciousness of my own right intentions, and by my dependence upon the protection of Almighty God. It will be my care to strengthen our institutions, civil a i ecclesiastical, bv discreet improvement, wherever improvement is required, and to do all in my power to compose and allay animosity and discord. " Acting upon these principles, I shall, upon all occasion;, look with confidence to the wisdom of parliament and the affections of my people, which form the true support of the of the constitution " dignity of the crown, and ensure the stability Then the Lord Chancellor, by her Majesty's command, said þÿ " My Lords and Gentlemen, " It is her Majesty's roval will and pleasure that this parliament he prorogued to Thursday, the 10th day of August next, to he then holdcu: and this parliament is accordingly prorogued to Thursday the 10th day of August next." Her Majesty had no sooner concluded, than the general remark throughout the house was " How admirably she delivered the

speech." The exclamations in the strangers' gallery, on the speech being ended, were, ' What a silvcrtoned voice I" " How gracefully she bears herself I" With what dignity she moves I" In short, numerous, energetic, and cordial were the culogiums pronounced on this, the fu st address to both houses of parliament, of our youthful Queen. Her Majesty then rose and quitted the house, attended in the same manner as on entering. She passed again down the royal gallery, and amid the acclamations of thousands and tens of thousands, returned to the palace. The House of Lords immediately broke up, and the peers, ambassadors, and the peeresses all came forth in a crowd. There was but one theme of the conversation of all, and that was the unaffected, simple, sensible, and dignified manner iu which the young Queen moved, looked, and spoke throughout the whole scene in which she had thus so conspi. cuously, and under such difficult circumstances (as they must surely be considered) comported herself. It was just three as the whole ceremony was concluded. þÿ Morning llerald, July 18.

A seaman' s prejudices against sailing on Friday. þÿ You see, when a man goes on observing that certain things always fall out just the "same way after other things happening, he must naturally put that and that together to make up his reckoning. Look here now ; 1 know the needle always points due north, allowing for variation is different in different places ; but so it is, and we steer our course accordingly. I ain't superstitous if I believe this, though can't account for I this. Well, and if I see the craft that sails on Friday goes to Davy's locker, while she that sails on Sunday makes a fair run, 1 say to myself Friday is an unlucky day. 1 don't call that superstitous a bit more than 1 call believing in the compass superstition ; to be sure, 'tisnt every one sees this, and they that don't know don't care; and certainly blessed are the ignorant for they know nothing. What happens in a craft belongs to a craft, d'ye see ; and a rotten timber laid in a ship when she is building, may cause more mischicl than a stiff gale or a heavy sea after she is launched, Now, a ship, to my thinking, is more like human being than just only a piece I of wood and iron put together in a builder's yard : a ship has almost as much life as a horse ; and when she founders she groans, poor thing, like a dying creature. Well, you sec, sir, if a fellow makes a had start at the beginning of a cruise, ' he never gets right till its over ; therefore, tis natural that the same should happen to a ship ; and I don't see why
it should not, for my part I was twice cast away on a Friday, and 1 don't like the day at all. þÿ Frazer's Mag.

Hiding Money in a Napkin. þÿ The great disposition at present manifested to collect specie and hide it awtry for future use, betrays a contracted mind and miserly disposition. If put to proper use and kept in circulation, those in possession of it would receive benefits of which the keeping of it close would forever deprive him. If he has a thousand dollars surplus, by investing it at six per cent interest, he finds himself in possession of two thousand, at the end of about sixteen years ;

whereas, if left unemployed, he reaps no benefit from it and it is entirely lost to him during that period. We give two instances which have fallen within our own knowledge, that may serve to illustrate our premises. The first was that of an old lady, who showed us a Lag of dollars which had been long kept locked in a strong box. The number amounted if we recollect aright, to three hundred. She informed us they were a present from a friend on the birth of her hoy. " And how old is the little rouge," we asked her. " Why there he is hoeing corn þÿ he was born the day of the battle of Lexington, and that makes him, fifty years, last April." " Rut have they never been put to interest, during that period ?" þÿ " Lord, dear suz, no ; they have never been out of this chamber and I set a3 much by them as the apple of my eye." The old lady lived several years afterward, fell into a state of fatuity, and her heirs reaped the benefit of that which she had -deprived herself the use of, and which would have contributed to her present necessities, and the comforts of life. The other case was that of a man of wealth. He had a trustworthy servant, whom he bade follow him down cellar. " Here, Paul," said þÿ he, " is a tea-kettle full of gold, which I want to reserve for a rainy day ; dig a hole, and cover it up ; no one knows or is to know, any thing about it. No accounts is made of it iu my books or papers and you are entrusted solely with the secret." Twenty years elapsed, and the merchant died. After an

inventory of his property had been taken, and his estate administered upon Paul, in the simplicity and honesty of his soul, took aside the executor of the will, related the circumstances, dug up the kettle, and restored its contents into the hands of its rightful owners. It is in justice due to the executors to say that he rewarded him for his fidelity by purchasing a farin and stocking it, which rendered him comfortably situated during life þÿ Gaz,

The Iiich Maris Daughter. þÿ It is often said that the times are strangely altered : and certain it is the people are. It was thought honorable to labor, to be constantly engaged in some active and useful þÿavocation but now-a-days it is thought honorable to be idle. There is much complaint of high prices of every necessary of humanexistence, and much truth. Hut if the amount of idleness could be calculated with mathematical accuracy throughout our extended republic, allowing the drones only halt price for services thev might perform, which others are now paid for, it might not be an unsafe calculation to put down the whole amount now paid for provisions and marketing in the United States. (From the Guiana Chronicle, August 2 5) letter from the earl of durham to the electors of north durham,

Sir, þÿ I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your communication of the 5th inst., in which you inform me of the proceedings of the electors of the north division of he county of Durham, at the meeting held on that day, and express a desire to ascertain my sentiments on the subject then brought under their consideration. In tiie first place, the nomination of a candidate should be the spontaneous act of the electors, and ought not to arise, fron. any influence or recommendation of mine. Secondly, a recurrence to the poll ought to be dependent on a strict examination of the registration returns. If the result of that inquiry gives you, as you state, a majority of a lesser amount, you ought unquestionably to enter into the contest, and yon shall have every support that 1 can constitutionally give you. On whichever side rests the majority, it ought to be wholly, not partially, represented. If it is Libeiai, by two Liberals : if Tory, bv two Tories . for I am decidedly opposed to all compromises tending to place the representation in political abeyance 1 his is not a moment when snpinencss or apathy can be tolerated. On the energies and determination of the Liberal party, in all classes, depend the destinies of the empire, A most glorious opportunity now presents itself of strengthening that great cause of reform and amelioration to which we have l.een so long devoted. A new reign has commenced. Our Sovereign, with all the cordial confidence of an open heart and generous feeling, lias
placed herself unreservedly in the hands of a

Liberal Government. Let us by our exertions justify that step, and add to their means of efficiently serving Her Majesty. Let us unite round her throne aii that is good, and wise, and patriotic in the empire. Let our watchwords þÿbe The « Queen and Liberty I The Queen and the Constitution ! The Queen and Reform ! Whatever principles ore most deai to us, most deeply implanted in the hearts of the people of England, may be, without reservation, indentificd with the name of the Soveieign. Educated by one of the best and w isest of her sex, her illustrious mother, our Queen knows that 110 throne is so secure as that which is based on the affections of its subjects þÿ no crown sits so lightly or so gracefully as that on which arc harmoniously blended the liberties of the people and the prerogatives of monarchy. As lor myself, as you have done me the honour, by desire oi the meeting, to ask my advice, I will tell you candidly what my views are. 'liiey aic what they have ever been, and are neither changed nor modified. I wish to rally as large a portion of the British people as possible around the existing institutions of the þÿcountry the Throne, Lords, Commons, and the Established Church. 1 do not wish to make new institutions, but to preserve and strengthen the old þÿ Herein iies the difference between nte and my opponents. Some would confine the advantages of those institutions to as small a class as possible ; 1 would throw them open to all who had the ability to comprehend, and the vigour to pro-

tect tlietn. Others, again, would annihilate them, for the purpose of forming new ones on fanciful and untried principles. I would 1 repeat, preserve them, but increase their efficiency, and add to the number ol their supporters. I have often stated the modes bv which, as I imagine, that efficiency can be most readily produced ; hut I have ever accompanied those declarations, as 1 do now. with the announcement of my determination never to force them peremptorily or dogmatically on the consideration ol the Government or the l'arliument If they are (as in mv conscience 1 believe them to be) useful and salutary þÿmeasures for they are based on the most implicit confidence in the loyalty and good feeling ol the people þÿ the course of events, and the experience of every day will remove the objections and prejudices which may now exist, and insure their adoption whenever they are recommended by the deliberate and determined voice of the people. 1 his, in a few words, is my political creed ; and no one can look for my co-operation or support oil aiiv other grounds. It lias been my ruling principle throughout my political life to endeavour to bring all classes þÿ especially the middle and lower, þÿ within the pale of the true, not the spurious, constitution. 1 have ever wished to give the latter an interest in the preservation of privileges, which exclusion would no longer render obnoxious to them ; to make them feel that whilst the (Town enjoyed its prerogatives, and the up-

per classes their honours, they also were invested with privileges most valuable to them ; and moreover, that all, separately and collectively, rested on the common basis of national utility. þÿ 1 remain. LONDON. ( From the Evening Mail, July 10.) I lie melancholy ceremonial of Saturday night, which closed the jaws of the tenth upon the ashes of our late Sovereign, will he found described elsewhere in all its details, ami will engage the attention of minds not qualified for meditation upon the intrinsic spirit of the scene itself, much less upon the nature of the awful event which gave rise to it. Funeral solemnities may he traced to the earliest ages of mankind, and have been exhibited according to their ditlereni modes by barbarous and by civilized nations þÿ bv the ancient Heathen, the modern savage, the II in don, the Mahometan, the Jew, and Christian. How far unimpassioned reason would suggest or justify such observances on the mere abandonment of the earthly body by its occupying and moving spirit is a question which ntcd not now he resolved The ostentatious burying or burning of the mortal remains of men lias grown out of the difficulty of altogether disconnecting in our notions, thefonn, though inanimate, from the living essence, or of reconciling with our habitual attachment to the concrete being, an entire disregard to that portion of it which aione the analyzing hand of death has left us. In our treatment of individuals of the highest rank þÿ Sovereigns or other great functionaries. who when alive are the visible representatives of national institutions þÿ it is useful to interest as much as possible t he imaginations of the multitude on the side of that pub-

lic Older and authority which such classes of functionaries have been appointed, and have so essentially contributed, to uphold. Hence come the reverential forms with which kings are surrounded during their life time, constituting a sort of halo, through which the mere human aspect, the personal necessities, infirmities, habits, and attributes of the Monarch are, in comparison with those of tiie hulk of his subjects, seen as through a gauze curtain, hut dimly and imperfectly. We are not sure, however, that a train <>f associations might not he encouraged through a skilful employment of those means w hich the decease of a sovereign places at the disposal oi iiis survivors more profoundly touch-

2)A1TSK jn<r, and serviceable to mankind, than any which the most gorgeous pomp or artificiu( pageantry is in its nature capable exciting. ol It seems to us, that whatever tends to the abatement of mortal pride, or produces a sense of the natural equality of all human creatures þÿ of the nothingness of material grandeur þÿ of the perishable tenure of created power þÿ of those humbling inflictions which are. common to iving and people, reducing all that is earthly to its own vile elements, and uplifting hopes the of rich and poor to a state of existence more exalted, independent, and enduring, would he the character most desirable to affix to the doposil any of mortal þÿ especially any royal þÿ fragments in the grave Our feeling is, therefore, that an extreme simplicity þÿ a simplicity approaching to that of the average of funerals in cases of ordinary þÿdeath ought to characterize the obsequies of a Christian monarch ; as little as possible ought to be done to separate in its outward appendages that which intrinsically is the same þÿ the death of one human being from another. Let it be in all cases just what decency requires not a pageant to be gazed þÿ upon by the lovers of stage spectacle þÿ but really and nakedly the burial of the dead. þÿ The nwfulness of the event þÿ the previous condition of the illustrious party þÿ the departure of the manl v spirit þÿ the closed windows of a million of free families, whose own unbought regret for their deceased friend and protector inclined them to make that honour-

able sacrifice þÿ viz, a suspension of the means by which tlicy lived þÿ the concern, moreover, universal among all ranks of those who were subjects of William IV., and who never, we believe, were bciore affected by a sympathy so m irked and general upon any one occasion siuce the death of the Princess Charlotte, 20 years ago þÿ the grateful and unquestionable testimony borne by the calm judgment of an enlightened nation to the solid virtues and endearing qualities of a King who redressed their grievances, consulted their wishes, mixed in their enjoyments, loved their Welfare, was alive to their glory, and gained, because he valued, their affections these were things þÿ which did, in truth, enhance, as well as constitute, the mournful splendour and deep solemnity of King William's funeral rites not the long þÿ train of public officers, the military hands, the crowns and cushions, tiie heraldic blazonings, the squadrons and battalions, the well-taught choir, the tolling bells, and booming guns, which spread over a circuit of some 50 miles the noisy notice of a King's interment. Farewell, then, William the just, the beneficent, and the true. No mean portion of your praise, O Kino ! is written in the acts of your predecessors. Your monument is the heart of a mighty people.

In like manner the lists of the estates must be made out with a true specification of the number of acres in canes, or in any other cultivation or pasture, the number of acres not used and the number of acres entirely useless þÿ In consequence whereof, the royal governments publication of the 26th of September 1833 is to he attended to ; Furthermore the names of the present owners, (as directed for the towns) together with the names of all the inhabitants without exception, are to he specified on the lists. For the convenience of the community, and in order to obtain as much regularity, as possible in the tax lists, schemes have been made printed by the Royal westindia government, which schemes will he delivered gratis for the town of Christianstaed and its Jurisdiction, at the burgher councils Incassator office and in Frederiksted and its J urisdiction at the police office of that town. It is a duty incumbent on every owner of a house to announce himself as such, in writing to the commission to prevent any doubt who is to pay the house tax ; and it is further directed, that owners of houses, that have been vacant or untenanted for six months or upwards, and in consequence thereof are entitled to get a proportional reduction in their taxes, are for that purpose, to come forward with sufficient proof of their assertion in order to enable the commissioners to observe the needful in the protocol ; in which respect the Commissioners refer to the royal Governments

publication of20tli October, 1830. It is to be observed, that the commission will receive no tax lists, except they are made out according to the above mentioned schemes and every column properly filled lip. It is however understood, that such lists are not required from owners oi houses, who have only to announce themselves as such to the commission, though not occupying their housces, as in such cases it will be considered sufficient when they announce themselves as such, together with the names of the persons who occupy the house, in writing to the commissioners. Separate lists duly signed by the owner or occupier for each house or plantation, is to be delivered to the commission notwithstanding the concerned individual might own morethan one house or plantation. All houses in both towns arc to be numbered, and the name of the streets to he placed on both sides of the cornerhuuses, painted with white on black ground or vice versa, in a conspicuous manner, according to Governor General v. Clausens placard of the 4th January 1777. In case of non compliance with the above, the following fines are to be paid and levied for : Ten Pieces of Eight for every list that is not rendered in due time, it be either in town or country, and proprietors, giving in lists which do not contain the explanations directed according to the beforemen tioned schemes will he subjected to the same fine, as the lists, in such cases will be returned to them. Owners of houses in towns, who neglect

announcing themselves as such in writing are liable to the same fine. 10 Ps. for every house number that is cither wanted or illegible, and the same for every streets name having the same defect. St. Croix, CHRISTIAN STED, ( THURSDA Y) November 1C, 1837. A remarkably large and brilliant Meteor exploded in a westerly dilection from us, on Sunday evening last, between 7 and 8 o'clock. The light caused by the Meteor, and the reflection thrown upon the houses, was similar to that cause I by a conflagration, and far exceeded the light of the Moon, then rising in the east.

The papers per first October packet, bringing London dates of the 2nd ultimo, furnish few articles of interest. Parliament would assemble on the 1 5th November ; the ministerial majority is ascertained to be 37 in the new house of Commons. Little is said of the a fairs of Portugal, Marshal Suldanha and the Duke of Terceira, having retreated to Santare.m. The Queen of Portugal was safely delivered of a Prince and heir to the crown, at Lisbon, in September. Don Carlos had pushed his Guerrillas almost to the gates of Madrid, but Espartero awaking from his lethargy, had marched forward. and encountered the Carlists on the 19/A September, when after some hard fighting, the tatter retreated into lower Arragon, followed by Espartero and Oroa, who had formed a junction þÿ the armies of each of the contending parties are nearly equal in numbers þÿ great dissention prevails in the Queens Government at Madrid. The remnant of the British Legion under þÿO Donnell who had advanced from St Seb ostia ns towards Tolosa, had suffered a severe defeat in company with the Queen's troops, \ were forced to retreat to Hernani ; 30 or 40 British officers were killed, and several hundreds were made prisoners. The French have again marched against Constantine in Africa, with 12,000 men þÿ the Duke De Nemours accompanies the expedition. The two daughters of the King of the French are affianced to the Prince of Wurtemberg, and to the hereditary Prince of Saxe Coburg, (both Protestants ) anti were, shortly to be mar-

ried. (From þÿBell Weekly s Messenger, August 2 0.) On Friday, Mrs Elisa Ann Frazer, flic widow of Captain Frazer, of the ship Stirling Castle, which was wrecked on a coral reef on the passage from Sydney to Sincapore, in INI ay, 1835, came to the Mansion-house, accompanied by the captain of the vessel in which she arrived in this country, and a female at whose house she was received upon coining to London, for the purpose of mentioning particulars the of her dreadful adventures amongst the inhabitants of the shores to which the crew resorted as a refuge from the not more appalling dangers of the ocean. The following is as close an account as our reporter could collect from a statement

On the 16th May, 1835, the Stirling Castle left Sydney for the purpose of going to Sincapore. On the 23rd, when they were ap- | behind. proaching Torres Straits, it blew very fresh, and there being a current near the Eliza ( 'oral lteefs, which the vessel was unable to resist, she struck on the reefs at about nine þÿo clock rent were dead at night, when the captain was incapable, on account of the hnzv weather, of making obserrations. There were about eighteen men | on board, two boys, and Mrs. Frazer, the þÿcaptain wife, s who was far advanced in pregnancy. Two of the men, who were labouring at the wheel, were killed when the ship struck, and the cabins were dashed into the hold, together with all the bread, beef, pork, and other provisions. The crew, when the tempest ceased, contrived to cut away the masts, in the expectation that the ship would right herself, by turning upon her beam ends, and she did, in some degree, change her position, but not to any serviceable extent. þÿ They, therefore, determined to get away as well as they could in the long boat and the pinnace, which they had contrived to keep secure, the two other boats, which were at-

by the fury of the elements. They knew that they were to the northward of Moreton Bay, a portion of the settlements of the English crown, and they determined to make for that place with as much expedition as possible. Accordingly, having worked with the most desperate industry until four o'clock on Sunday, they disembarked from the vessel and took to the boats. The þÿship c s arpenter, the cook, the cook's mate, John Frazer, the - the men of their clothes, captain's nephew, the boatswain, Edward Stone, and Bill Lorton, a seaman, took to the pinnace, while the captain, his wife, the chief and second mates, 'the two boys, arid the rest of the crew, took to the long boat, four days after they committed themselves to the care of Providence, Mrs. Frazer was delivered of a child while up to her waist in water in the long boat. 'I he infant was born alive, but after a few gasps was drowned, and the first lieutenant wrapped up the body in a part of Ins shirt, which he tore from his back for the purpose, and Ft it go along with the tide. The poor mother could not account for the extraordinary vigour with which she was able to bear up against this calamity, added to the other calamities n> which she was doomed to be exposed. 1 ortunalelv she was for some tune in a state ol insensibility, and

SiASTSX T33!T'Jira>2SZ Hi3MMKMUme8 AT33. was not, until n considerable time after the child was consigned to the deep, aware that it was brought into a world from which it was so rapidly hurried away. For a great many days they endeavoured in vain to reach Moreton Bay, being all the time without any food, except a small quantity of the lees of hops which they had found in a cask. They suffered dreadfully from thirst us well as hunger while in this awful situation. At last they reached a large rock, to which they fastened their boats, and they went in quest of oysters and water, but their disappointments were multiplied upon them, and they stretched themselves along in expectation of a speedy release from their sufferings bv the interposition of another tempest. In the morning those who belong to the long boat were astonished to find that the pinnace, and the men j who had occupied her, had altogether disap- j peared. These unfortunate fellows were never heard of more, and their comrades in calamity could not conjecture what their mo- ) necessarily confused and incoherent : þÿ tive could be for making an experiment by ( themselves, without the aid of the experience of the captain and his mates, whom they left

The captain's aim was all along, after they had been obliged to quit the ship, to reach Moreton Bay, but finding that wind and curagainst his object, and bis companions being reduced to the extremity I of lying on their backs in the boat, with their tongues out, to catch the damp of the dew that fell, lie resolved to make for the nearest land. It was a choice of most awful evil, for lie knew that the shores which it was probable they would reach was visited by tribes of j savages They bore away before the wind, prepared to meet dealh in whatever shape it might present itself, and so exhausted with suffering as to be careless whether they were to die by the bands of the natives or to be overwhelmed in the waves. At last they came within sight of land, and soon afterwards their boat ran into, and landed in, a place called Wale Bay. They were now | within about 100 miles to the north of Moreton Bay, which is the principal of the settlements to which the incourageable convicts tached to the ship, having been swept away , are sent to pass the remainder of their davs in uniiitcrmilted labour, and just as lliev touched the land they caught a siglil of vast crowds ot naked savages, who soon approached the beach, evidently delighted with the prize that presented itself. The savages surrounded the boat, and, raising it up, carried it from the beach to the bush with its crew just as they were. The moment they laid the boat on the ground they began to strip commencing with ,

the captain and chief officers. John Baxter, the second mate, endeavoured to hide a shirt ornament, in which his aunt's hair was contained, having willingly yielded up every tiling else, but the savages became infuriated at the attempt at concealment, and beat him j dreadfully, ft is unnecessary to say that they tore tlie trinket away from him. They broke in pieces the watches and cliroriomctors, and each took a portion of the machinery to slich in their noses and ears, and after they had divided amongst themselves the various portions of apparel of which they hud | stripped their captives they threw to them, to appease their hunger, the heads and guts of the fish upon which they had been lately making their meal. The savages, alter having detained them two days, took them furtlier up into the bushes, and drove them on-

ward, that they might, ns they soon ascertained, fall into the hands of other tribes, by whom an ingenious variety was to be given to their sufferings. The captain bad endeavoured to prevail upon them to accept the services of the poor crew for a longer time, being apprehensive that any change amongst the natives would be for the worse ; but they beat all the now naked whites on before them, until fresh tribes came up and took each of them a prisoner, and set him to work in carrying pieces of trees, and toiling in other exhausting ways. Mrs Frazer, being the only woman, was not selected by any of the tribes, but was left by herself, while they all went onward ; but her husband got an opportunity to mention to her not to stir from the place in which she was at the moment, and that be would contrive to see her in a lew hours. During that night she lay in the clefts of a rock, and ill the morning, after looking about without seeing a creature, she determined to follow some foot-marks, and, after having proceeded to some distance, she saw a crowd of black women approach. These women belonged to the tribe of savages by whom her husband bad been taken up the bush on the proceeding day, and they set fier to work in trailing wood and lighting fires. Being quite naked, and presenting a contrast in her skin which the women did not like, she was compelled by them to rub herself all over with gum and herbs, w hich had the effect of making her nearly as dark as themselves. They

likewise tattooed her all over, and, having pulled her hair out, covered her head with a sort of gutn, and stuck the feathers of paired and other birds all over it. One of the women, having two children, obliged her to nurse one of them, notwithstanding the severe labour she had to perforin ; and if the child was out of temper, the nurse was kicked, and scratched, and thumped for its peevishness. At the expiration ot four days Mrs. Frazer saw hei husband for the first time since their separation. De was dragging along a tree, and was greatly fatigued. She find first begun to inquire bow it happened that lie did not manage to let her know where be w as. to which he was replying that lie dare not look for her, when his tribe suddenly appeared. þÿ One of them, having seen them together, made a push at the captain with a spear and pierced him right through the body, which was a corpse in an instant. Mrs. Frazer ran to her husband, cried out þÿ Jesus of Nazareth, I can endure this no longer," and pulicd the spear out of the body, but the breath was gone for ever. She then fell senseless, and remained so for a considerable time, and when she recovered her senses, site found herself along with the tribe, which site was obliged to serve ; but what became of the body of captain Frazer she could never learn, and, of course, the- barbarous region in which she was enslaved, was no place for sympathy. Shortly after this catastrophe, the first officer of the ship having been informed that the

captain bad been murdered by one of the tribes, formed, in a fit of desperation, a plan ol revenge, fettered, and exhausted with labour as lie was. His intention was, however, discovered, and horrible was bis punishment. Mrs. Frazer bad just lighted a fire bv order ol her tribe, and the unlbilunate þÿman s legs were thrust into it and consumed, while he, by the violence of his contortions, actually worked for the rest ol bis body a grave in the sand, in which it was embedded.
